questions.question: What is the difference between a function declaration, a function expression and an arrow function in terms of hoisting and use?
questions.answer:
A function declaration (function greet() {}) is hoisted completely — both the name and the body — so it can be called on a line above its definition. A function expression assigns a function to a variable, so it follows that variable's rules: with const it sits in the temporal dead zone until the assignment and calling it earlier throws ReferenceError; with var the name hoists as undefined and calling it throws TypeError. Arrow functions are always expressions, so they are never callable before their assignment.

Beyond hoisting, arrows have no own this, no arguments and cannot be used with new. Declarations are good for top-level named helpers and for mutual recursion; expressions keep a helper scoped and make it obvious it is a value; arrows are best for short callbacks and transforms.
key_points: Declarations hoist name + body — callable before definition
const expressions are in the TDZ; var expressions are undefined
Arrows are expressions with no this, arguments or new
Use declarations for named helpers, arrows for callbacks

questions.answer:
It prints 5, then undefined.

Default parameters are used only when the argument is undefined. null is not undefined, so b stays null; then 5 + null evaluates to 5 because null coerces to 0 in numeric addition. The default looks like it should protect you but it never ran. If you need to treat null like missing, use b ?? 10 inside the body (nullish coalescing) rather than a default parameter.

The second function returns undefined because of automatic semicolon insertion: a newline directly after return ends the statement, so the function returns nothing and the 5 is unreachable dead code. JavaScript does not warn about this. Keep the value on the same line as return.
key_points: Defaults fire only for undefined, not null/0/""/false
5 + null is 5 because null coerces to 0
Use ?? in the body for null-safe defaults
A newline after return triggers ASI → undefined

questions.question: When should you use an arrow function instead of a normal function? What do arrows give up?
questions.answer:
Use an arrow when you want a short expression, when you want to keep the surrounding this (array callbacks, class field handlers, a function inside a method), or when you do not need a dynamic this. Arrows inherit this lexically from the enclosing scope, so an arrow inside an object method still sees the method's this — which is exactly what you want for setTimeout(() => this.count++).

Arrows give up four things: their own this (so they cannot be used as object methods that need the object), their own arguments object (use rest parameters), the ability to be called with new (they have no prototype and throw TypeError), and the ability to be used with call/apply to rebind this. They are also not hoisted as declarations, since they are always expressions.
key_points: Arrows inherit this lexically — great for callbacks and timers
No own arguments → use ...args
Cannot be constructed with new
call/apply/bind cannot change an arrow's this
Avoid arrows for object methods that need this

questions.answer:
greet("Kakade") is a function call, not a function reference. It runs immediately, returns undefined, and setTimeout receives undefined as its callback — so the greeting prints right away and nothing is scheduled. The fix is to pass a function that will call greet later: setTimeout(() => greet("Kakade"), 1000), or setTimeout(greet, 1000, "Kakade") to forward the argument.

The second line is the same class of bug in reverse: map passes (element, index, array) to console.log, so it logs three lines like 1 0 [1,2,3]. console.log accepts extra arguments, which is why it does not crash — but it is not printing what the author expected. Wrap callbacks that take extra parameters: .map((n) => console.log(n)).
key_points: Pass a function reference, not the result of calling it
setTimeout(fn, delay, ...args) can forward arguments
map/filter/forEach callbacks receive (element, index, array)
Extra arguments are silently accepted by many functions

questions.question: What makes a function pure, and why does purity matter for testing and for array methods?
questions.answer:
A pure function has two properties: given the same arguments it always returns the same result, and it has no side effects. Side effects include mutating an argument or an outer variable, writing to the DOM, logging, network calls, reading Math.random() or Date.now(), and throwing exceptions for control flow. A function that pushes into the array it was given is impure even if it also returns the array, because the caller's data changed.

Purity matters because pure functions are trivially testable (no mocks, no setup), safe to cache (memoization is only valid if the output depends solely on inputs), safe to run in parallel, and easy to compose. Array methods like map, filter and reduce are designed around pure callbacks: if the callback mutates shared state, you get order-dependent bugs, especially when the code later moves to a different engine or async context.
key_points: Same input → same output, every time
No mutation, I/O, randomness, or time reads
Pure functions are easy to test, cache and compose
Mutating callbacks break map/filter/reduce assumptions
